not_recognised: The question is not recognised, please try asking other question.

intents.title: Getting started
examples: I am new, how do I use this app
how do I get started with my exercises
intents.answer: Here is how to start: 1) Make sure your health profile is complete (Profile tab), so your safety limits are set. 2) Open AI-assisted treatment planning and tap Retrieve physical treatment to get plans that suit you, then select one. 3) Open My treatment plan from the Treatment tab and start the first exercise: read its steps, then record yourself doing it. 4) The app checks your posture; reach 80% to move on to the next exercise. Your reminders follow the plan's weekly schedule.

intents.title: How to do the exercises
examples: how do I do the exercises
what is the correct way to do this exercise
how do I know my form is right
am I doing the exercise properly
intents.answer: Each exercise in your plan has its own steps and safety points: open it from your treatment pathway. Move slowly and smoothly, keep breathing, and stay within a comfortable range. Record yourself doing it and the app will check your posture and tell you what to correct. You can also ask me how to do a specific exercise, for example "how do I do the heel raise?"

intents.title: Pain or discomfort
examples: my knee hurts when I exercise
is it normal to feel sore after exercising
what should I do if I feel pain
my muscles ache the next day
intents.answer: Some muscle tiredness or mild soreness for a day or two is normal when you start, and it should ease as you get used to the exercises. Pain that is sharp, gets worse while you exercise, or comes with swelling is not normal. Which describes your pain best? Choose an option below.

intents.title: How often and how long
examples: can I do this every day
how long should each session be
what time of day is best
intents.answer: Follow the number of sessions per week shown in your plan, with a rest day in between when you can. Each session only takes a few minutes, and any time of day that suits you is fine, as long as it is not straight after a big meal. Your reminders already follow this schedule. Doing the exercises well matters more than doing extra sessions.

intents.title: Missed a session
examples: what if I skip a day
intents.answer: That is fine. Do your next session as usual; do not do two sessions in one day to catch up. If you have missed several days, start again gently with fewer repetitions and build back up.

intents.title: Exercising safely
examples: is it safe for me to exercise
do I need to warm up
intents.answer: Exercise next to a sturdy chair or counter, on a dry non-slip floor, and breathe normally; never hold your breath. Warm up with a few minutes of gentle movement first. Stop if you feel dizzy, short of breath, or unwell. Your plan already stays within the safety limits from your health profile.

intents.title: Exercising with a health condition
examples: I have diabetes, is there anything special I should do
can I exercise with high blood pressure
intents.answer: Your plan was chosen within the safety limits for the conditions in your health profile, so you can follow it as set. Stop and rest if anything feels wrong, and check with your doctor before doing more than the plan.

intents.title: What you need
examples: what kind of chair should I use
do I need to buy anything
can I do it on the bed
intents.answer: You do not need to buy anything. Most exercises use a firm chair without wheels or armrests, pushed against a wall; a sofa or bed is too soft. Floor exercises need a mat or a carpet, and step-ups need a low step (no higher than 15 cm) with a rail. Wear comfortable clothes and non-slip shoes. A small water bottle can be used as a light weight if you are comfortable.

intents.title: Too easy or too hard
examples: this is too hard for me
I can't finish all the repetitions
intents.answer: If an exercise is too hard, do fewer repetitions with good form and rest between them; it should feel like effort, not pain. If you cannot move as far as the picture, go only as far as is comfortable and a little further each week. If it feels too easy, keep the same plan until you finish it, then request a new recommendation from the planning page: it will suggest a plan for your new level. Do not add weight, extra sets or other exercises on your own.

intents.title: Feeling tired or unwell
examples: I feel too tired to exercise
I am exhausted after the session
should I exercise when I am sick
intents.answer: Feeling a little tired after exercising is normal. If you are unusually exhausted, unwell, or have a fever, skip today's session and rest; continue when you feel better. If tiredness lasts for days or comes with breathlessness, contact your doctor.

intents.title: Weak or unsteady legs
examples: my leg feels wobbly when standing
I feel unsteady on my feet
intents.answer: Legs, arms or hands that feel weak, wobbly or shaky are common after a long period of less activity, and this is what your exercises are building up. For standing exercises always keep one hand on a sturdy chair or counter; for any exercise do fewer repetitions and rest when the shaking starts. If weakness comes on suddenly, or affects one side of your body, stop and get medical help straight away; if your hand shakes even when it is resting, tell your doctor.

intents.title: Recording your exercise video
examples: how do I record my exercise
where should I put my phone
the app cannot detect my body
why does it say my full body is not visible
how long should the video be
intents.answer: Put your phone on a stand, upright, at about waist height and 2.5 to 3 metres away, so your whole body from head to feet stays in the picture during the movement. Use good light in front of you and record 10 to 30 seconds. Each exercise says whether the camera should face you or be at your side. Someone else may hold the phone for you if it stays still. If the app cannot see your whole body, step back a little and record again. If it found no repetition, make each movement a little bigger and slower, with a short pause back at the start.

intents.title: Understanding your posture score
examples: what does my posture score mean
what do I do if I fail the posture check
intents.answer: The posture score shows how closely your movement matched the correct form, as a percentage, with tips on what to change. At 80% or more your progress is updated automatically. Below that you can read the tips and retry, or continue; every attempt is saved so you can see your improvement. If it counted fewer repetitions than you did, make each one a full, clear movement with a short pause back at the start, and keep your whole body in the picture.

intents.title: When to exercise
examples: when is the best time to exercise
is it ok to exercise at night
should I exercise in the morning or evening
intents.answer: The best time is when you feel alert and have had a light meal about an hour before. Many people find late morning or late afternoon easiest. Keep to a regular time so it becomes a habit, and avoid the last hour or two before bed.

intents.title: How the app works
keywords: how do i use this app
examples: how do I use this app
intents.answer: HealthGuide has five tabs. Home shows today's session and your daily limits. Treatment holds your plan: get one in AI-assisted treatment planning, then do each exercise and record it so the app can check your posture. Profile holds your health details, which keep your advice safe. You can ask me about any of these at any time. You need an internet connection to sign in, check your posture and chat with me; your reminders still arrive without one.

intents.title: Your doctor's advice
examples: my doctor said I should rest for a week
the physiotherapist told me not to do squats
intents.answer: Always follow your doctor's or physiotherapist's advice first: it is based on examining you. If they told you to rest, pause your exercises (you can switch reminders off) and continue when they say it is safe; your progress is kept. If their advice differs from your plan, ask them which exercises are suitable, and update your health profile if anything has changed.

intents.title: Clicking or cracking joints
examples: my shoulder clicks when I raise my arm
my knee makes a cracking sound
intents.answer: Clicking or cracking without pain is common and usually harmless; it is often gas or a tendon moving over the joint. Carry on if it does not hurt. If it comes with pain, swelling, or the joint catching or locking, stop that movement and ask your doctor or physiotherapist.

intents.title: My treatment plan
examples: take me to my treatment plan
intents.answer: Your treatment plan shows your exercises in order. Open the next one, read its steps, then record yourself doing it; the app checks your posture and moves you on when you reach 80%.

intents.title: Your health profile
examples: how do I update my health profile
why is my risk level high
how do I change my weight
where can I add my health conditions
intents.answer: Your health profile holds your age, gender, weight, height, health conditions and physical limitations. Your risk level and safety limits are worked out from it, and your treatment plans are chosen to fit them. Tap the button below, then Edit, to change anything; keep it up to date so your advice stays safe.

intents.title: Exercise reminders
examples: how do I change my reminder time
how do I turn off reminders
how do I change the days of my reminder
how do I delete a reminder
intents.answer: An exercise reminder says which exercise is next, and tapping it opens that plan. Open Reminders to change things: tap the time to change it, and tap a day to turn it on or off; one day must stay on, so to stop a reminder, switch it off instead. “Remind me to log my health readings” adds a daily reminder to record your blood pressure, sugar or weight. Reminders you added yourself can be deleted with the bin button; a plan's reminders stay with the plan and stop when the plan stops. If none arrive, check that notifications are allowed for HealthGuide in your phone settings. If you have already exercised that day, that day's exercise reminder is skipped. The sound follows your phone's notification settings.

intents.title: The possible-fall message
examples: the app said I may have fallen
why did I get a fall warning
intents.answer: The posture check saw a movement that looked like losing your balance or a fall. If you did fall, or feel hurt or dizzy, stop and get help; call 999 in an emergency. If it was a false alarm (for example you bent down to pick something up), you can record the exercise again. Keep a sturdy chair or counter within reach while you exercise.

intents.title: Adjusted targets
examples: what does targets adjusted to my health profile mean
intents.answer: Because of your age or health profile, the posture check asks for a little less range of movement, so the exercises stay safe and achievable while your strength comes back. Checks on how you move, such as keeping your elbows straight or your back upright, are the same for everyone. If your health has changed, update your profile.

intents.title: Partial repetitions
intents.answer: The posture check saw you moving but not as far as a full repetition, so it counted partial repetitions. That is a fine start, especially after a long rest: move a little further each session, only as far as is comfortable, and pause briefly back at the start of each one.

intents.title: Video too dark or too far
examples: it says my video is quite dark
why does it say move the phone closer
intents.answer: A dark video, or you looking small in the picture, makes the posture check less accurate. Record with a light on in front of you (not behind you), and place the phone about 2 to 3 metres away so your whole body fills most of the picture, from head to feet.

intents.title: Languages
intents.answer: I answer in English and understand many everyday Malay words mixed in, such as sakit, lutut, boleh or penat. Short, simple sentences work best. In an emergency, call 999.

intents.title: Exercising for a family member
examples: can my mother do these exercises
is this plan suitable for my father
intents.answer: Each person should use their own account and health profile: the plan and its safety limits are chosen from the profile of the person exercising, including their age, conditions and fall risk. Help them create an account and fill in their profile, then get a plan for them. For an older family member, stay close during the first sessions, keep a sturdy chair or counter within reach, and set up the phone for them so the app can check their posture. If they have fallen in the past year, feel unsteady or have a heart condition, ask their doctor before they start.

intents.title: Weak muscles after bed rest
examples: I was in hospital for weeks and my legs are weak
my muscles shrank after bed rest
is it too late to build muscle at my age
intents.answer: Muscles shrink quickly after weeks in bed or in hospital, but they grow stronger again with exercise at any age. Start with the easiest exercises in your plan, a few repetitions with a sturdy chair within reach, and add a little each week; most people notice a difference within 4 to 8 weeks. Eat some protein at each meal (fish, eggs, tofu, beans or milk) unless your doctor has limited it. If one calf is swollen, warm or painful after bed rest, see a doctor before exercising.

intents.title: Afraid of falling
examples: I am scared I will fall
what if I fall when nobody is home
intents.answer: Being afraid of falling is common. Keep one hand on a sturdy chair or kitchen counter, wear non-slip shoes, clear the floor and keep your phone within reach. If you live alone, do the standing exercises when someone is at home, and skip them on days you feel unsteady. If you fall, do not get up quickly: rest, check for pain, roll onto your side, crawl to a sturdy chair and push up slowly. If you are hurt or cannot get up, call for help or 999 and keep warm. Tell your doctor about any fall or near-fall; they can check your balance and medicines.

intents.title: Text too small
examples: how do I make the text bigger
intents.answer: The app follows your phone's text size. To make the words bigger, open your phone's Settings, then Display, then Font size (on some phones, Font size and style), and move the slider up; the app's text grows with it. A family member can also sit with you while you use the app.

intents.title: Help from family
examples: can my daughter help me with the app
can my caregiver record my video
intents.answer: Yes. A family member or carer can set up the phone, record your video, and read your results and my answers with you. Keep using your own account and health profile so your plan stays matched to you, and do the exercises yourself; they can stay close by in case you lose your balance.

intents.title: Eating and exercise
examples: I make myself vomit after eating
I haven't eaten for 2 days, can I exercise
I skip meals so I can exercise more
intents.answer: Please eat regular meals and do not exercise on an empty stomach or to make up for what you ate: your body needs food to recover and to keep you steady. If you have not been able to eat for a day or more, rest today and talk to your doctor. If you feel you have to make yourself vomit, skip meals or exercise to control your weight, you are not alone: talk to your doctor, or call Befrienders KL 03-7627 2929 (24 hours) or Talian HEAL 15555 (8 am to midnight). I cannot give calorie or weight-loss advice.

intents.title: Leaking urine
examples: I wet myself a little when I do the squats
urine leaks out when I cough or squat
intents.answer: Leaking a little urine when you squat, cough or lift is common, especially after childbirth or as we get older, and it can be treated. Empty your bladder before you exercise and tell your doctor or a physiotherapist: pelvic floor exercises often help. If it starts suddenly together with back pain or numbness between your legs, get medical help straight away.

intents.title: Feeling low
examples: my husband died and I feel so sad
intents.answer: I am sorry you are feeling this way. Low mood is common during recovery and after a loss, and it is not a weakness. Gentle activity, daylight and talking with someone you trust can help. If you have felt low or lost interest in most things for more than two weeks, please talk to your doctor. If you ever think about harming yourself, call Befrienders KL 03-7627 2929 (24 hours) or Talian HEAL 15555 (8 am to midnight), or 999 in an emergency.

intents.title: Exercising in hot weather
examples: it is very hot, can I exercise?
is it ok to exercise in hot weather
intents.answer: On hot days exercise indoors in a cool, airy room, or outdoors only before 11 am or after 4 pm. Drink water before and after, wear light clothes, and stop if you feel dizzy, very thirsty, very sweaty or get a headache. Older adults and people with heart disease or diabetes are more at risk in the heat, so take extra care.

intents.title: Keeping motivated
examples: I feel too lazy to exercise
intents.answer: Many people feel this way. Start small: do just the first exercise today, at the same time each day, and let your reminder prompt you. Exercising with a family member helps, and Results shows how far you have come. Strength comes back slowly after a long rest, so every session counts, even a short one. If you have felt low or lost interest in most things for more than two weeks, please talk to your doctor.

intents.title: Other sports and activities
examples: can I go to the gym
intents.answer: Gentle walking is good for you, also on rest days: on even ground, with your walking aid if you use one, and with someone if you have fallen before. For harder activity such as jogging, sports or the gym, wait until your plan has built up your strength, start gently, and ask your doctor or physiotherapist first, especially if you have a health condition or have fallen before. Stop if it causes pain that is still there the next day.

intents.title: Your past results
examples: where can I see my past results
how did I do in my last session
intents.answer: Every exercise you record is saved with its posture score and tips. Session history shows them all, with your average, your best score and a chart of how your posture accuracy is changing.

intents.title: Following more than one plan
examples: can I follow two plans at the same time
how many plans can I have
why does it say the plan clashes
the same exercise is in both my plans
intents.answer: You can follow more than one plan: up to 3 at a time if your risk level is Low, 2 if it is Medium, and 1 if it is High. Two plans with the same goal that train the same joints clash, so the app asks you to replace one instead of adding the second; a shoulder plan and a hand plan can be followed together. Each plan gives you one exercise a day; an exercise that is in two of your plans is done once and counts for both. To add a plan, open AI-assisted planning and choose Retrieve physical treatment. To stop one, open it on the Physical Treatment page and tap Stop this plan; your progress so far is kept.

intents.title: Neck problems
examples: why can I not select my neck
is there an exercise for my neck
intents.answer: This app does not include neck exercises, which is why the neck is greyed out on the body map: neck problems need a doctor or physiotherapist to guide the exercises. If you have neck pain, see your doctor or physiotherapist, and get medical help straight away if it comes with numbness, tingling or weakness in your arms, or after a fall or injury. If your neck hurts during another exercise, stop that exercise and tell your doctor or physiotherapist.

intents.title: Choosing the body area
examples: how do I choose the part I want to recover
can I choose more than one part
is there any exercise for my hand
intents.answer: Open AI-assisted planning and choose Retrieve physical treatment. The first question shows a body figure: tap each part you want to recover (you can choose more than one; its name appears on the picture), tap it again to remove it, and use Front and Back to turn the figure. If you cannot find the place, tap “Can't find it? Choose from a list”. The plans suggested then focus on the parts you chose; wrists and hands have their own plan, Hand and Wrist Recovery. The neck is greyed out: neck problems need a doctor or physiotherapist, so the app has no neck exercises.

intents.title: “Does not look like” the exercise
keywords: legs moved one at a time
examples: it says this video does not look like the exercise
why does it say wrong exercise
it said my arm went backwards
intents.answer: The posture check first makes sure the video shows the exercise you chose. When it says the video does not look like that exercise, nothing is saved and the reason in brackets says what looked different, for example “your arm went backwards, not forwards”. Check that you picked the exercise you recorded, then record it again following its steps, with the phone where the exercise says (in front of you or at your side) and your whole body in the picture. If you are sure it was the right exercise, try again with slower, clearer movements.

intents.title: Changing your password
examples: how do I change my password
I want a new password but I know the old one
intents.answer: To change your password while you still know it, open Profile and tap Change password: type your current password, then the new one twice (at least 8 characters, with a letter and a number). Your other phones are then signed out; this one stays signed in. If you have forgotten your current password, tap “Forgot your current password?” there, or Forgot password? on the login screen, to get a reset code by email.

intents.title: Why you were logged out
examples: why do I have to log in again
intents.answer: To keep your health details safe, you stay signed in on this phone only while you use the app: after 3 days without opening it you are signed out, and you log in again with your email and password (or Continue with Google). Opening the app at least once every 3 days keeps you signed in. Changing or resetting your password also signs you out on your other phones.

intents.title: Reminders that come late or not at all
examples: why did my reminder come late
how do I turn on notifications
intents.answer: If the Reminders page says notifications are turned off, tap Turn on notifications, switch them on for HealthGuide and come back to the app: your reminders are set again (this also fixes pressing Don't allow by mistake). If reminders come late, Android may hold them back by up to an hour to save battery. To get them on time, open your phone's Settings, find HealthGuide under Apps (on some phones under Special app access) and turn on Alarms & reminders, then close and reopen HealthGuide.

intents.title: A reminder to log your health readings
examples: can I get a reminder to log my blood pressure
remind me to record my health readings
intents.answer: Yes. Open Reminders and tap “Remind me to log my health readings”: it reminds you every day at 8 pm to record your blood pressure, sugar or weight, and it is never skipped. Tap the time or the days to change them, switch it off for a while, or delete it with the bin button.

intents.title: Leaving an exercise
examples: how do I stop the exercise halfway
how do I exit the recording
intents.answer: Tap Exit at the top of the recording, analysing or result screen to stop the exercise and go back to the home page. While you are recording or the video is being checked, the app asks first, and that attempt is not saved; a result of 80% or more that was already saved stays saved. You can do the exercise again later from Physical Treatment. If you feel pain, dizziness or unwell, stop at once, sit down and rest.

intents.title: Signing in with Google
examples: I signed in with Google, why does it ask for a password
what happens if I cancel the account setup
intents.answer: You can sign in with Continue with Google on the login screen. The first time, the app asks you to complete your account: choose a username and a password (at least 8 characters, with a letter and a number), so you can also log in with your email and password later. If you tap Cancel, nothing is kept and you return to the login screen; you can start again any time. If your Google email already has an account here, Google is linked to it and the app says “Your Google account has been linked to your existing account.”: your plans and results stay as they are.

intents.title: Changing your plan or reminders
examples: how do I change my plan
can I get a different plan
how do I stop this plan
intents.answer: To change plan, open AI-assisted planning and choose Retrieve physical treatment to get new recommendations. You can follow up to 3 plans at once, depending on your risk level; a new plan for the same body area and goal replaces the one you have. You can stop a plan from the Physical Treatment page with Stop this plan. Reminders follow your plan's weekly schedule; check that notifications are allowed for the app in your phone settings if they do not appear.

intents.title: Forgot password
examples: how do I reset my password
intents.answer: You can set a new password with a 6-digit code sent to your email: tap the button below (or Forgot password? on the login screen), enter your email, then type the code and your new password. If the code does not arrive, check your spam folder and wait a minute before asking for a new one. After too many wrong passwords the account is locked for 15 minutes.

intents.title: Verification code
examples: I did not get the verification code
how do I verify my email
intents.answer: The 6-digit code is sent to the email you registered with. Check your spam or junk folder, and make sure the address is spelled correctly. You can tap Resend code once a minute; a code stops working after a while, and after 5 wrong tries (the app then says it has expired), so tap Resend code and always use the newest one. If you clicked a link in the email instead, return to the app and log in.

intents.title: Account and login
examples: how do I update my health profile
intents.answer: Log in with the email and password you registered with, or use Continue with Google. If you forgot your password, tap Forgot password? on the login screen to get a reset code by email. You can update your health details on the Profile page; your plan's safety limits are recalculated when you save. Your data is only visible to your own account.

intents.title: Mild soreness or tiredness
examples: my muscles are a bit sore the next day
intents.answer: Mild soreness is a normal sign that your muscles are working. Keep exercising gently, move within a comfortable range, and it should ease within a day or two. If it lasts longer than three days, do fewer repetitions and contact your physiotherapist.

intents.title: Sharp or worsening pain
examples: I get a sharp pain during the exercise
intents.answer: Stop the exercise that causes it and rest. Do not push through sharp or worsening pain. If it does not settle within a day, or it stops you moving normally, contact your doctor or physiotherapist before you continue with that exercise.

intents.title: Swelling, redness or heat
examples: my knee is swelling after exercise
the joint looks red and feels warm
intents.answer: Stop exercising that joint and rest it, raised if you can. Swelling, redness or heat in a joint should be checked: contact your doctor or physiotherapist before exercising it again. If the swelling is severe or you also have a fever, seek medical care today.

intents.title: Medicines
examples: can I take painkillers before exercising
intents.answer: I cannot give advice about medicines. Please ask your doctor or pharmacist, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed unless they tell you otherwise. If a dose was taken twice by mistake, call your pharmacist or doctor now for advice; for insulin, a blood thinner or many tablets, call 999.

intents.title: Diagnosis and seeing a doctor
examples: what is wrong with my knee
intents.answer: I cannot diagnose conditions or injuries. If you are worried, or a problem is not improving, please see your doctor or physiotherapist about it. If you think something is broken or seriously injured, stop exercising it and get medical care.

intents.title: Food and drink
examples: what should I eat before exercising
can I exercise after a meal
intents.answer: Drink some water before and after your exercises, and wait about an hour after a large meal before exercising. For food advice that suits your health conditions, use the Diet section of the app.

intents.title: Greeting
intents.answer: Hello! I can answer questions about your rehabilitation exercises, pain, safety, your plan, recording your videos and reminders. Tap a topic below or type your question.

intents.title: Thanks
intents.answer: You're welcome. Keep it up! Ask me anything else about your plan, or tap Exit Chatbot when you are done.

intents.title: Okay
intents.answer: Okay. If you have another question about your exercises, pain, safety or your plan, type it or tap a topic below.

intents.title: Goodbye
intents.answer: Take care, and see you at your next session. Tap Exit Chatbot to return to the planning page.

intents.title: About this assistant
intents.answer: I am the rehabilitation assistant for your treatment plan. I answer common questions using answers prepared in advance, so I cannot diagnose or give medical advice. You can ask about how to do your exercises, pain, safety, how often to exercise, recording your video, your posture score, and your plan or reminders.

intents.title: Why plans stop at 65
keywords: too old to get a plan
not allowed to get a plan
why can i not get a plan
why can't i get a plan
examples: why can't I get a plan
am I too old for a plan
intents.answer: Exercise plans are for users under 65. From 65 the app does not create plans, and a plan you already have is paused, as stated in the Terms of Use (section 2): the home exercise programmes proven for people aged 65 and over were set up and followed by a health professional, and this app has none. Exercise is still good for you: please ask your doctor or a registered physiotherapist to set up a programme, or ask about a hospital or community rehabilitation service. Your profile, health logging, past results and this chat assistant stay available.

intents.title: Your data and privacy
examples: who can see my health information
do you keep my exercise videos
how long do you keep my data
intents.answer: Only you can see your data: each account can read only its own records, and it is not sold or shared with anyone. Your profile, plans, results, chat messages, reminders and logged readings are kept on our database provider's servers (Supabase) in Singapore. Exercise videos are checked and deleted straight after the check; only the score, repetitions and feedback are kept. Your data is kept while you use the app, and an account not used for 2 years is deleted with its data. You can correct your data in the app, ask for a copy at elwinksy-wm23@student.tarc.edu.my, or delete your account. The full Privacy Notice is in Profile, Terms of Use and Privacy Notice.

intents.title: Deleting your account
examples: how do I delete my account
I want to remove my account and data
can I undo deleting my account
intents.answer: Open Profile and tap Delete my account (the last item under Account settings), then confirm. Your account and everything saved with it (profile, plans, results, chat messages and reminders) is deleted at once, and this phone's reminders are cancelled. It cannot be undone: to use the app again you would register as a new user. Deleting your account also withdraws your consent to the use of your health information.

intents.title: Terms of Use
examples: where can I read the terms
why must I accept the terms again
what happens if I decline the terms
intents.answer: You can read the Terms of Use and Privacy Notice any time in Profile, in English or Malay. They say what the app is (not a doctor or physiotherapist), who can use it (13 and over; plans only under 65), how to exercise safely, how plans are chosen and how your data is kept. When they change, the app shows the new version at your next login and you need to accept it to continue. If you decline, you are signed out and cannot use the app, but your account is not deleted.

intents.title: Users under 18
examples: I'm 15, can I use this app
why does my parent need to agree
I turned 18, how do I change my age group
intents.answer: You can use the app from 13. Under 18, a parent or legal guardian must read the Terms and agree to them, and to the use of your health information, on the Terms screen; their name is recorded. If your age in the profile does not match the age group you chose in the Terms (for example you have turned 18), the profile asks you to tap Review Terms and choose your age group again before it saves.

intents.title: Checking with your doctor first
examples: why can't I get a plan, it says check with my doctor first
my doctor said OK, how do I get a plan
intents.answer: Some conditions ask in your health profile whether they are under control (for example asthma or blood pressure). Under control means your symptoms are stable with your usual treatment and your doctor has not told you to avoid exercise. If you answered No for a condition that needs it, the app does not make a new exercise plan until your doctor agrees, because exercise could make it worse. When your doctor says it is OK, open Profile, change that answer to Yes and save; then you can get a plan again.

intents.title: Reporting a wrong answer
examples: how do I report a wrong answer
intents.answer: Sorry about that. Tap Report this answer under the answer, and if you can, say what you expected and which topic you meant. Reports are read and checked by the team before anything in my answers changes. You can also try asking in other words, or pick a topic below.

intents.title: Why a plan was chosen
examples: why was this plan chosen for me
what are the sources under the reasons
intents.answer: Each plan card has Why this plan: tap it to see why the plan suits you (the body area, your recovery stage, your goal) and the safety rules it meets. Under the plans, Why not the other plans lists each plan that was left out and why, for example harder than your safety limit or for another body area. Each reason shows the guideline behind it; tap Source to read the full reference. App safety rule means a rule of this app itself, set to keep you safe, with no published guideline of its own.

intents.title: Your risk level
examples: what does my risk level mean
intents.answer: Your risk level comes from your health profile. Low: no health conditions or physical limitations. Medium: one condition that is under control, or an arm or leg limitation. High: two or more conditions; a heart, blood pressure, stroke or nerve condition (such as Parkinson's); a condition that is not under control; or a balance problem. A higher level means gentler limits: shorter, easier sessions, smaller movement targets in the posture check and fewer plans at once. It is not a diagnosis, and it is worked out again whenever you save your profile, so keep it up to date. Your BMI (weight divided by height squared) is shown for information; it does not change your risk level.

intents.title: Your safety limits
examples: why is my session only 20 minutes
intents.answer: Your safety limits come from your risk level: low risk, up to moderate intensity and 45 minutes a session; medium risk, up to moderate intensity and 30 minutes; high risk, up to low intensity and 20 minutes. Plans with harder exercises or longer sessions are left out, and Why not the other plans says so. Home also shows daily limits for food (calories, salt and sugar) worked out from your profile. They are recalculated when you save your profile.

intents.title: The planning questions
examples: which mobility level should I choose
intents.answer: Treatment planning asks: the area that needs rehabilitation (on the body map or from the list); how far along your recovery is (Early: just started recovering; Intermediate: some movement is back; Advanced: nearly back to normal); how well you can move (Low: need support to move; Moderate: move slowly on my own; High: move freely); your main goal (build strength, move more freely, better balance, ease pain or more stamina); and, if you like, your pace (Gentle, about 3 days a week; Steady, about 4; Faster, about 5). If you are not sure, choose the lower option: plans for a later stage or a higher mobility level than yours are left out, so the lower choice is the safer one.

intents.title: The exercise animation
examples: what is the moving figure in the exercise
intents.answer: The moving figure shows one repetition of the exercise, made from recordings of it done correctly. Copy its range and its slow, steady pace; you can go slower than it if you need to. It is shown with the exercise's steps and in the camera view before you record. If it does not appear, close the exercise and open it again; an exercise without one yet (Wrist Extension) has only its written steps.

intents.title: Health Connect and devices
examples: how do I connect my smartwatch
intents.answer: Health Connect is Android's app for sharing health data, such as steps or heart rate from a smartwatch or fitness band. Profile, Device connection shows whether it is linked. Linking a device comes with the app's Health Monitoring part, which is not available in this version yet. You do not need a watch for your exercises: the posture check only uses your phone's camera.

intents.title: About the app
keywords: will it work on my phone
examples: can I use it on iPhone
intents.answer: HealthGuide is free. It is a university final-year project prototype for evaluation, made for Android phones with a camera and an internet connection; there is no iPhone version. On an older phone the posture check may take longer, but it works the same. For help, or about your data, email elwinksy-wm23@student.tarc.edu.my.

intents.title: Tell me a bit more
intents.answer: Could you tell me a bit more about what you mean? For example: "how do I do the heel raise?", "why is my posture score low?" or "is it safe to exercise with knee pain?". You can also pick a topic below.

intents.title: Not closed
intents.answer: “Not closed” in your posture result means your hand did not close into a fist between openings. Between openings, close your hand into a gentle fist.

intents.title: Arm leg low
examples: what does arm leg low mean
the result said arm leg low
intents.answer: “Arm leg low” in your posture result means your arm and leg did not reach the level of your back. Stretch your arm and leg a little further, towards the level of your back, only as far as feels steady.

intents.title: Back arch
intents.answer: “Back arch” in your posture result means your lower back bent backwards as your arms went up. Keep your back still; do not lean backwards as your arms go up.

intents.title: Back sag
intents.answer: “Back sag” in your posture result means your lower back dipped or your hips tilted while you stretched. Keep your back flat and your hips level.

intents.title: Bent elbow
intents.answer: “Bent elbow” in your posture result means your elbows were bent while your arms were raised. Keep your elbows straight as you lift.

intents.title: Bent knee
intents.answer: “Bent knee” in your posture result means the knee of your lifting leg was bent. Keep the knee of the lifting leg straight.

intents.title: Body swing
intents.answer: “Body swing” in your posture result means you rocked your body back to help lift. Keep your body still; do not rock back to lift.

intents.title: Drop down
intents.answer: “Drop down” in your posture result means you came down from the step too quickly. Step down slowly, holding the rail, and let your foot touch down gently.

intents.title: Feet far
intents.answer: “Feet far” in your posture result means your feet were too far from your buttocks. Bring your feet closer to your buttocks.

intents.title: Feet forward
intents.answer: “Feet forward” in your posture result means your feet were too far in front of you when you started to stand. Bring your feet back so your knees are above your ankles before you stand.

intents.title: Feet not in line
examples: what does feet not in line mean
the result said feet not in line
intents.answer: “Feet not in line” in your posture result means your feet were side by side or apart instead of one in front of the other. Place one foot directly in front of the other, heel touching toe.

intents.title: Hands used
intents.answer: “Hands used” in your posture result means your hands pushed on your legs or the chair to help you stand. If you can, stand up with your arms crossed; if you need your hands to stand safely, that is fine.

intents.title: Heels lift
intents.answer: “Heels lift” in your posture result means your heels came off the floor. Keep your heels on the floor.

intents.title: Hips back
intents.answer: “Hips back” in your posture result means your hips were pushed back, so your body bent at the hips. Keep your body straight; do not push your hips back.

intents.title: Hips sag
intents.answer: “Hips sag” in your posture result means your hips dropped towards the wall, so your body was not straight. Keep your body straight from head to heels.

intents.title: Incomplete extension
intents.answer: “Incomplete extension” in your posture result means your knee did not straighten fully. Straighten your knee so your leg is straight out in front, as far as is comfortable.

intents.title: Incomplete stand
intents.answer: “Incomplete stand” in your posture result means you did not stand up fully straight at the top. Stand up fully: straighten your hips and knees at the top, as far as you safely can.

intents.title: Fingers not spread
examples: what does fingers not spread mean
the result said fingers not spread
intents.answer: “Fingers not spread” in your posture result means your fingers stayed close together when your hand opened. Spread your fingers wide as you open your hand, only as far as is comfortable.

intents.title: Head tilt
intents.answer: “Head tilt” in your posture result means your head tilted to one side as you lifted. Keep your head level and look straight ahead.

intents.title: Knee not straight
examples: what does knee not straight mean
the result said knee not straight
intents.answer: “Knee not straight” in your posture result means your leading leg was not fully straight at the top of the step. Straighten your leading leg at the top, holding the rail, as far as is comfortable.

intents.title: Knees bend
intents.answer: “Knees bend” in your posture result means your knees bent as you rose onto your toes. Keep your knees straight as you rise.

intents.title: Leaning
intents.answer: “Leaning” in your posture result means you leaned on the counter or to the side. Stand upright with a light touch on the counter, rather than leaning your weight on it.

intents.title: Leaning back
intents.answer: “Leaning back” in your posture result means you leaned your upper body backwards. Sit or stand tall; do not lean back.

intents.title: Leaning forward
intents.answer: “Leaning forward” in your posture result means you leaned your upper body forwards. Keep your upper body upright.

intents.title: Leg forward
intents.answer: “Leg forward” in your posture result means your leg went forwards instead of straight out to the side. Lift the leg straight out to the side, not forwards.

intents.title: Low hips
intents.answer: “Low hips” in your posture result means your hips did not lift high enough. Lift your hips a little higher, towards a straight line from shoulders to knees, without pain in your back.

intents.title: Low knee lift
examples: what does low knee lift mean
the result said low knee lift
intents.answer: “Low knee lift” in your posture result means your knees did not lift high enough. Lift your knees a little higher, only as far as is comfortable.

intents.title: Low raise
intents.answer: “Low raise” in your posture result means your heels did not rise high enough. Rise a little higher onto your toes, holding the chair, only as far as feels steady.

intents.title: Low range
intents.answer: “Low range” in your posture result means the movement did not go as far as the exercise asks. Move a little further each time, as far as is comfortable; the exercise steps say how far.

intents.title: No arm swing
examples: what does no arm swing mean
the result said no arm swing
intents.answer: “No arm swing” in your posture result means your arms stayed still while you marched. If you feel steady, swing your arms as you march; if not, keep one hand on the chair.

intents.title: No forward lean
examples: what does no forward lean mean
the result said no forward lean
intents.answer: “No forward lean” in your posture result means you did not lean your chest forward before standing up. Lean your chest forward a little before you stand up.

intents.title: No hold
intents.answer: “No hold” in your posture result means you did not hold the top position. Pause and hold for about 2 seconds before lowering.

intents.title: Over arch
intents.answer: “Over arch” in your posture result means your hips went too high, so your lower back arched. Do not push your hips too high; keep your lower back from arching.

intents.title: Shoulder shrug
intents.answer: “Shoulder shrug” in your posture result means your shoulders lifted up towards your ears. Relax your shoulders down, away from your ears.

intents.title: Slouching
intents.answer: “Slouching” in your posture result means you slumped or leaned back away from the chair back. Sit up straight with your back against the chair.

intents.title: Stepping out
intents.answer: “Stepping out” in your posture result means you stepped out of position during the hold. If you wobble, step out or hold the counter: that is the safe thing to do. With practice you will hold it for longer.

intents.title: Swinging
intents.answer: “Swinging” in your posture result means you swung your arms up quickly instead of lifting slowly. Lift slowly and pause at the top instead of swinging.

intents.title: Thigh lift
intents.answer: “Thigh lift” in your posture result means your whole thigh lifted off the seat. Keep your thigh resting on the seat; only the lower leg moves.

intents.title: Toes up
intents.answer: “Toes up” in your posture result means your toes turned up or outwards as the leg lifted. Keep your toes pointing forwards.

intents.title: Too deep
intents.answer: “Too deep” in your posture result means you bent your knees further than a mini squat. Only bend your knees a little, about a third of the way down.

intents.title: Trunk forward
intents.answer: “Trunk forward” in your posture result means you bent forward at the waist. Stand tall and keep your chest up.

intents.title: Trunk lean
intents.answer: “Trunk lean” in your posture result means your body leaned to the side. Keep your body upright; do not lean to the side.

intents.title: Uncontrolled sit
intents.answer: “Uncontrolled sit” in your posture result means you sat down too quickly instead of lowering yourself slowly. Sit down slowly: reach back for the chair with your hands and lower yourself gently.

intents.title: Uneven arms
intents.answer: “Uneven arms” in your posture result means one arm went higher than the other. Lift both arms together to the same height.

intents.title: Upper arm moves
examples: what does upper arm moves mean
the result said upper arm moves
intents.answer: “Upper arm moves” in your posture result means your upper arm moved away from your side. Keep your upper arms still against your body.

intents.title: Using hands
intents.answer: “Using hands” in your posture result means your hands pulled your leg up. Lift your legs without pulling them up with your hands.

sit_to_stand.name: Sit-to-Stand
sit_to_stand.instruction: Sit on a firm chair with feet flat and hip-width apart. Lean slightly forward and stand up fully without using your hands, then sit back down slowly. Safety: keep a stable chair against a wall; stop if you feel dizzy or knee pain.
sit_to_stand.camera: side view, whole body in frame

shoulder_abduction.name: Shoulder Abduction
aliases: raise my arms to the side
shoulder_abduction.instruction: Stand tall with arms by your sides. Raise both arms out to the side up to shoulder height with elbows straight, hold for one second, and lower slowly. Safety: do not raise above a pain-free range.
shoulder_abduction.camera: facing you, whole body in frame

shoulder_flexion.name: Shoulder Flexion
shoulder_flexion.instruction: Stand with arms by your sides. Raise both arms forward and up to shoulder height with elbows straight and thumbs up, hold for one second, and lower slowly. Safety: do not arch the back.
shoulder_flexion.camera: side view, whole body in frame

hip_abduction.name: Standing Hip Abduction
aliases: lift my leg to the side
hip_abduction.instruction: Stand beside a chair and hold it for support. Lift one leg out to the side keeping the toes forward and the body upright, then lower it. Repeat on the other side. Safety: do not lean the trunk.
hip_abduction.camera: facing you, whole body in frame

knee_extension.name: Seated Knee Extension
knee_extension.instruction: Sit upright on a chair. Straighten one knee until the leg is level with the hip, hold for two seconds, and lower slowly. Alternate legs. Safety: keep the back against the chair.
knee_extension.camera: side view, whole body in frame

elbow_flexion.name: Elbow Flexion
elbow_flexion.instruction: Stand or sit with arms by your sides, palms forward. Bend the elbows to bring the hands toward the shoulders, keeping the upper arms still against your body, then lower slowly. Use a light bottle of water if comfortable. Safety: keep the weight light and stop if the elbow or shoulder hurts.
elbow_flexion.camera: side view, whole body in frame

wall_push_up.name: Wall Push-Up
wall_push_up.instruction: Stand an arm's length from a wall with palms on the wall at shoulder height. Bend the elbows to bring the chest toward the wall, then push back. Safety: keep the body straight from head to heels.
wall_push_up.camera: side view, whole body in frame, wall at one edge of the picture

heel_raise.name: Heel Raise
heel_raise.instruction: Stand behind a chair holding the back of it. Rise onto your toes, hold for one second, and lower slowly. Safety: keep holding the chair throughout.
heel_raise.camera: side view, whole body in frame

mini_squat.name: Mini Squat
mini_squat.instruction: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding a support. Bend the knees about 30 degrees keeping the heels down and the chest up, then stand up. Safety: knees must not pass the toes.
mini_squat.camera: side view, whole body in frame

seated_marching.name: Seated Marching
seated_marching.instruction: Sit upright on a chair without leaning back. Lift one knee toward the chest, lower it, and alternate legs at a steady pace. Safety: use a sturdy chair without wheels, with your feet flat on the floor between lifts.
seated_marching.camera: side view, whole body in frame

glute_bridge.name: Glute Bridge
glute_bridge.instruction: Lie on your back on a mat with knees bent and feet flat. Squeeze the buttocks and lift the hips until shoulders, hips and knees are in a straight line, then lower slowly. Safety: do not arch the lower back.
glute_bridge.camera: side view, phone on the floor about 2 m away, whole body in frame

tandem_stance.name: Tandem Stance
aliases: one foot in front of the other
tandem_stance.instruction: Stand next to a counter. Place one foot directly in front of the other, heel touching toe, and hold for 30 seconds. Switch feet. Safety: always keep one hand near the support.
tandem_stance.camera: facing you, whole body in frame

bird_dog.name: Bird Dog
bird_dog.instruction: Kneel on a mat on hands and knees, hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Stretch one arm forward and the opposite leg back until both are level with your back, hold for two seconds, return, and switch sides. Safety: keep the back flat, do not twist.
bird_dog.camera: side view, phone on the floor about 2 m away, whole body in frame

step_up.name: Step-Up
step_up.instruction: Stand facing a low step holding a rail. Step up with one foot, straighten that leg fully, bring the other foot up, then step down slowly. Alternate the leading leg. Safety: use a step no higher than 15 cm.
step_up.camera: side view, whole body and the step in frame

march_in_place.name: March in Place
march_in_place.instruction: Stand tall and march on the spot, lifting the knees to hip height if comfortable and swinging the arms, at a steady pace. Safety: stay near a wall or sturdy chair you can hold, and stop if you feel dizzy or very short of breath.
march_in_place.camera: side view, whole body in frame

wrist_extension.name: Wrist Extension
wrist_extension.instruction: Sit at a table and rest your forearm on it with the hand over the edge, palm down. Slowly lift the hand up as far as is comfortable, keeping the forearm on the table, then lower it. Safety: stop if it hurts or tingles.
wrist_extension.camera: at table height on the side of your arm, forearm and hand in the picture

hand_open_close.name: Hand Open and Close
hand_open_close.instruction: Sit at a table with your forearms resting on it. Make a gentle fist, then open and spread your fingers as wide as is comfortable, and close the hand again slowly. Safety: stop if it hurts or tingles.
hand_open_close.camera: facing you at table height, your hands in the picture

condition_notes.HYPERTENSION: Because you have high blood pressure: breathe out as you lift and never hold your breath, and stop if you get a headache, blurred vision or feel dizzy.
condition_notes.DIABETES: Because you have diabetes: keep a sugary drink or snack nearby and stop if you feel shaky, sweaty or confused, which can mean low blood sugar. Wear well-fitting shoes and check your feet afterwards.
condition_notes.HEART_DISEASE: Because you have heart disease: warm up first, keep to the intensity in your plan, and stop straight away if you feel chest discomfort, unusual breathlessness or a racing heartbeat.
condition_notes.STROKE: Because you have had a stroke: exercise next to a sturdy support, go slowly on your weaker side, and stop if you notice new weakness, numbness or difficulty speaking.
condition_notes.ARTHRITIS: Because you have arthritis: some joint stiffness at the start is normal; move within a comfortable range and do not push into sharp joint pain.
condition_notes.OSTEOPOROSIS: Because you have osteoporosis: avoid twisting or bending forward sharply, and keep a support within reach to prevent falls.
condition_notes.ASTHMA: Because you have asthma: keep your reliever inhaler nearby and stop if you start wheezing or your chest feels tight.
condition_notes.PREGNANCY: Because you are pregnant or have recently given birth: do not lie flat on your back after the first months, keep a support nearby, drink water and do not overheat; stop and contact your doctor or midwife if you have bleeding, dizziness, pain or leaking fluid.
condition_notes.JOINT_REPLACEMENT: Because you have had a joint replacement: your surgeon's and physiotherapist's movement advice comes first, and stop if the joint becomes red, hot, swollen or more painful.
condition_notes.RHEUMATOID_ARTHRITIS: Because you have rheumatoid arthritis: move within a comfortable range, and during a flare rest hot, swollen joints and do fewer repetitions.
condition_notes.COPD: Because you have chronic lung disease: go at a pace where you can still speak, breathe out slowly through pursed lips, and stop if you are too breathless to talk.
condition_notes.CANCER: Because you have or had cancer: follow your doctor's advice on exercise during treatment, go gently on tired days, and stop if you have new bone pain, a fever or unusual tiredness.
condition_notes.KIDNEY_DISEASE: Because you have kidney disease: keep to a comfortable, moderate effort, drink as your kidney team advises, and on dialysis days ask them when it is best to exercise.
condition_notes.PARKINSONS: Because you have Parkinson's disease: exercise next to a sturdy support, take your time when standing up and turning, and stop if you feel unsteady.
condition_notes.MULTIPLE_SCLEROSIS: Because you have multiple sclerosis: keep cool (a fan, cool water, a cool room), rest between sets, and stop if your symptoms get worse; they usually settle once you cool down.
condition_notes.FOOT_ULCER: Because you have a foot ulcer or wound: do your exercises sitting or lying, keep weight off the foot, and check your feet every day.
condition_notes.OTHER: Because of the other condition in your profile: follow your doctor's advice on exercise, and stop if anything feels wrong.

limitation_notes.BALANCE_IMPAIRMENT: Because you declared a balance limitation: always keep one hand on a sturdy support.
limitation_notes.LEFT_LEG_MOBILITY: Go gently with your left leg and keep a support within reach.
limitation_notes.RIGHT_LEG_MOBILITY: Go gently with your right leg and keep a support within reach.
limitation_notes.LEFT_ARM_MOBILITY: Only move your left arm within a range that feels comfortable.
limitation_notes.RIGHT_ARM_MOBILITY: Only move your right arm within a range that feels comfortable.

risk_notes.High: Your risk level is High: follow your plan exactly as set and check with a healthcare professional before doing more.

late_night_note: It is {time} where you are. Late at night is not a good time for your exercises: tiredness and dim light raise the risk of a fall, and activity close to bedtime can disturb your sleep. Rest now and do them tomorrow, ideally in the late morning or late afternoon.

DIABETES.evening: With diabetes, avoid exercising late in the evening: it can make your blood sugar drop overnight. Exercise earlier in the day, about 1 to 3 hours after a meal.
DIABETES.late_night: With diabetes, exercising at night can make your blood sugar drop while you sleep.
DIABETES.early_morning: With diabetes, avoid exercising on an empty stomach first thing; have breakfast and exercise about 1 to 3 hours after it.
DIABETES.daytime: With diabetes, exercise about 1 to 3 hours after a meal rather than on an empty stomach.

HYPERTENSION.early_morning: Blood pressure is naturally higher in the first hours after waking: wait about an hour after you get up, warm up slowly and keep the effort gentle.

HEART_DISEASE.early_morning: Heart strain is more likely in the early morning: wait about an hour after waking, warm up slowly and avoid exercising right after a large meal.

ARTHRITIS.early_morning: Joints are often stiffest first thing in the morning: a warm shower and a few gentle movements first, or exercising later in the morning, can make it easier.

ASTHMA.early_morning: Cool morning air can trigger asthma: exercise indoors and warm up gradually.
ASTHMA.late_night: Cool night air can trigger asthma, another reason to wait until tomorrow.

OSTEOPOROSIS.early_morning: Make sure the room is well lit and the floor is clear: falls are more likely when you have just woken up.
OSTEOPOROSIS.evening: Make sure the room is well lit and the floor is clear: falls are more likely when it is dark or you are tired.

STROKE.evening: Exercise when you are not tired, with good lighting and someone nearby if possible.

BALANCE_IMPAIRMENT.early_morning: With your balance limitation, wait until you are fully awake and steady, and keep the room well lit.
BALANCE_IMPAIRMENT.evening: With your balance limitation, exercise in a well-lit room with someone nearby if possible.

now_notes.early_morning: It is {time} where you are. Early morning is fine once you have been up for a while, had something light to eat and warmed up.
now_notes.daytime: It is {time} where you are, a good time for your exercises if you feel well and have not just eaten a large meal.
now_notes.evening: It is {time} where you are. A session now is fine; finish at least an hour or two before bed so it does not disturb your sleep.

condition_detail.HYPERTENSION: With high blood pressure, regular gentle exercise like your plan can help lower it over time. Breathe out as you lift and never hold your breath or strain. If a home reading is 180/110 or higher, do not exercise that day: rest and contact your doctor.
condition_detail.DIABETES: With diabetes, exercise helps control your blood sugar. If you take insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar, check your level before you start and have a small snack if it is low; keep glucose sweets nearby, and stop if you feel shaky, sweaty or confused. Check your feet afterwards.
condition_detail.HEART_DISEASE: With heart disease, keep to the intensity in your plan: you should still be able to talk while exercising. Warm up and cool down for about five minutes. Stop at once if you get chest discomfort, unusual breathlessness, dizziness or a racing heartbeat, and call 999 if it does not settle with rest.
condition_detail.STROKE: After a stroke, these exercises help you regain strength and balance. Do them next to a sturdy support, go slowly on your weaker side, and stop and call 999 if you notice new weakness, numbness, a drooping face or slurred speech.
condition_detail.ARTHRITIS: With arthritis, moving keeps your joints flexible and the muscles around them strong. Some discomfort is fine if it settles within about two hours; if it lasts longer, do fewer repetitions next time. Rest a joint that is hot and swollen during a flare.
condition_detail.OSTEOPOROSIS: With osteoporosis, strengthening and standing exercises help your bones. Avoid bending forward from the waist, twisting and jerky movements, and keep a support within reach to prevent falls.
condition_detail.ASTHMA: With asthma, warm up gradually and keep your reliever inhaler within reach; use it before exercising if your doctor has told you to. Stop if you start wheezing or your chest feels tight, and avoid exercising in cold air or when your asthma is not well controlled.
condition_detail.PREGNANCY: During pregnancy, gentle exercise is usually safe and helpful when the pregnancy is going well, but check with your doctor or midwife first. After the first three months avoid lying flat on your back for long (as in the glute bridge), exercise on a firm, non-slip surface with a support nearby for balance, drink water and do not overheat. Stop and contact your doctor if you have bleeding, dizziness, chest pain, calf pain or swelling, contractions or leaking fluid.
condition_detail.JOINT_REPLACEMENT: After a hip or knee replacement, your surgeon's and physiotherapist's exercises and precautions come first: they decide how far you may bend and when you may do more. After a new hip, avoid bending it past 90 degrees (a right angle), crossing your legs and twisting, and keep the leg facing forward, until they say it is safe. Ask them before starting this plan, and stop if the wound becomes red, hot, swollen or more painful, or you get calf pain or a fever.
condition_detail.RHEUMATOID_ARTHRITIS: With rheumatoid arthritis, regular exercise is part of standard care: it keeps your joints moving and the muscles around them strong. Move within a comfortable range; during a flare, rest hot, swollen joints, do fewer repetitions and build up again as it settles.
condition_detail.COPD: With chronic lung disease, exercise improves your breathing and strength. Go at a pace where you can still speak, breathe out slowly through pursed lips, and rest between sets. Stop and contact your doctor if you are much more breathless than usual, cough up blood or have chest pain.
condition_detail.CANCER: During and after cancer treatment, staying active helps with tiredness and strength, but follow your doctor's advice first, especially during treatment. Go gently on tired days, and stop and tell your doctor if you have new bone pain, a fever, or feel unusually tired or breathless.
condition_detail.KIDNEY_DISEASE: With chronic kidney disease, regular moderate exercise is recommended as you can manage it. Keep to a comfortable effort, drink as your kidney team advises, and on dialysis days ask them when it is best to exercise. Stop if you feel dizzy, breathless or have chest pain.
condition_detail.PARKINSONS: With Parkinson's disease, strength and balance exercises help you move more easily and confidently. Exercise next to a sturdy support, take your time when standing up and turning, and stop if you feel unsteady or about to fall.
condition_detail.MULTIPLE_SCLEROSIS: With multiple sclerosis, strength exercises help, but heat can make symptoms worse for a while. Keep cool with a fan, cool water and a cool room, rest between sets, and stop if symptoms get worse; they usually settle once you cool down. During a relapse, rest and ask your doctor before starting again.
condition_detail.FOOT_ULCER: With a foot ulcer or an open wound on the foot, do not put weight on it: do your exercises sitting or lying until it has healed, check your feet every day, and see your doctor if the wound gets bigger, red, hot or smelly.
condition_detail.SURGERY_WOUND: A little oozing from a surgical wound can be normal in the first days, but if it keeps bleeding, soaks the dressing, or turns red, hot, swollen or smelly, or you get a fever, contact your surgeon or clinic today, and do not exercise that area until they have checked it.
condition_detail.INJURY: With a recent fracture, sprain or a cast, do not exercise the injured part until your doctor or physiotherapist says it is ready. Exercises that do not use it are usually fine, but check with them first, and stop if the injured area hurts or swells.

condition_closing: Your plan was chosen within the safety limits set from your health profile, so follow it as set and check with your doctor before doing more.

diet_notes.HYPERTENSION: With high blood pressure, keep salt low: your daily sodium limit is on the Home page.
diet_notes.DIABETES: With diabetes, spread carbohydrates through the day and exercise 1 to 3 hours after a meal; your daily sugar limit is on the Home page.
diet_notes.HEART_DISEASE: With heart disease, keep salt and saturated fat low and avoid exercising after a large meal.

If you are in danger now or might act on these thoughts, call 999 or go to the nearest emergency department. red_flag_answer: Stop exercising now. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, sudden weakness or numbness, slurred speech, or severe swelling, call 999 or go to the nearest emergency department. For other new pain, dizziness or a fall, sit down, rest, and contact your doctor before exercising again.

AGE_65_PLUS.title: Your plans are paused
AGE_65_PLUS.answer: Your exercise plans are paused because plans are for users under 65, as stated in the Terms of Use (section 2). The home exercise programmes proven for people aged 65 and over were set up and followed by a health professional, and this app has none. Please ask your doctor or a registered physiotherapist to set up a programme for you, or ask about a hospital or community rehabilitation service. You can still use your profile, health logging, reminders to log your health readings, your past results and this chat assistant.
AGE_65_PLUS.note: Your plans are paused (plans are for users under 65, Terms of Use section 2), so please exercise under the guidance of your doctor or a physiotherapist.
